claim: The gene regulatory network (GRN) that underlies echinoderm skeletogenesis is a prominent model of GRN architecture and evolution.
source: The gene regulatory network (GRN) that underlies echinoderm skeletogenesis is a prominent model of GRN architecture and evolution.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field, supported by established scientific consensus.

claim: KirrelL is an essential downstream effector gene in the echinoderm skeletogenic network.
source: KirrelL is an essential downstream effector gene in this network and encodes an Ig-superfamily protein required for the fusion of skeletogenic cells and the formation of the skeleton.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: KirrelL encodes an Ig-superfamily protein required for the fusion of skeletogenic cells and the formation of the skeleton.
source: KirrelL is an essential downstream effector gene in this network and encodes an Ig-superfamily protein required for the fusion of skeletogenic cells and the formation of the skeleton.
evidence: This is supported by functional studies referenced in the manuscript.

claim: The study dissected the transcriptional control region of the kirrelL gene of the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus.
source: In this study, we dissected the transcriptional control region of the kirrelL gene of the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus.
evidence: This describes the experimental work performed in the study.

claim: Key cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and transcription factor inputs that regulate Sp-kirrelL were identified using plasmid- and bacterial artificial chromosome-based transgenic reporter assays.
source: Using plasmid- and bacterial artificial chromosome-based transgenic reporter assays, we identified key cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and transcription factor inputs that regulate Sp-kirrelL, including direct, positive inputs from two key transcription factors in the skeletogenic GRN, Alx1 and Ets1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sp-kirrelL receives direct, positive inputs from Alx1 and Ets1.
source: Using plasmid- and bacterial artificial chromosome-based transgenic reporter assays, we identified key cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and transcription factor inputs that regulate Sp-kirrelL, including direct, positive inputs from two key transcription factors in the skeletogenic GRN, Alx1 and Ets1.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis and ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: kirrelL cis-regulatory regions were identified from seven other echinoderm species representing all classes within the phylum.
source: We next identified kirrelL cis-regulatory regions from seven other echinoderm species that together represent all classes within the phylum.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Heterologous kirrelL regulatory regions from seven echinoderm species drove PMC-specific expression in developing sea urchin embryos.
source: By introducing these heterologous regulatory regions into developing sea urchin embryos we provide evidence of their remarkable conservation across ~500 million years of evolution.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: kirrelL regulatory regions are remarkably conserved across ~500 million years of evolution.
source: By introducing these heterologous regulatory regions into developing sea urchin embryos we provide evidence of their remarkable conservation across ~500 million years of evolution.
evidence: This is supported by functional conservation demonstrated in transgenic assays.

claim: The kirrelL regulatory region of the sea star, Patiria miniata, receives direct inputs from Alx1 and Ets1.
source: We dissected in detail the kirrelL regulatory region of the sea star, Patiria miniata, and demonstrated that it also receives direct inputs from Alx1 and Ets1.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis of the Pm-kirrelL regulatory region.

claim: kirrelL is a component of the ancestral echinoderm skeletogenic GRN.
source: Our findings identify kirrelL as a component of the ancestral echinoderm skeletogenic GRN.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of kirrelL regulatory regions across diverse echinoderm species.

claim: GRN subcircuits, including specific transcription factor–CRE interactions, can remain stable over vast periods of evolutionary history.
source: They support the view that GRN subcircuits, including specific transcription factor–CRE interactions, can remain stable over vast periods of evolutionary history.
evidence: This is supported by the conservation of Alx1 and Ets1 inputs into kirrelL across echinoderms.

claim: The analysis of kirrelL establishes direct linkages between a developmental GRN and an effector gene that controls cell–cell fusion.
source: Lastly, our analysis of kirrelL establishes direct linkages between a developmental GRN and an effector gene that controls a key morphogenetic cell behavior, cell–cell fusion, providing a paradigm for extending the explanatory power of GRNs.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of direct transcriptional inputs from GRN components into kirrelL.

claim: Sea urchins and other echinoderms are prominent models for GRN biology.
source: Sea urchins and other echinoderms are prominent models for GRN biology for several reasons: (1) there are well-developed tools for dissecting developmental GRNs in these animals, (2) a large number of species that represent a wide range of evolutionary distances are amenable to study, and (3) there is a rich diversity of developmental modes and morphologies within the phylum (Arnone et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and established knowledge in the field.

claim: All adult echinoderms possess elaborate, calcified endoskeletons.
source: All adult echinoderms possess elaborate, calcified endoskeletons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about echinoderm anatomy.

claim: Most echinoderm species are maximal indirect developers that develop via a feeding larva that undergoes metamorphosis to produce the adult.
source: Most species are maximal indirect developers; that is, they develop via a feeding larva that undergoes metamorphosis to produce the adult.
evidence: This is established knowledge about echinoderm development.

claim: The feeding larvae of echinoids (sea urchins) and ophiuroids (brittle stars) have extensive endoskeletons.
source: The feeding larvae of echinoids (sea urchins) and ophiuroids (brittle stars) have extensive endoskeletons, holothuroids (sea cucumbers) have rudimentary skeletal elements, and asteroids (sea stars) lack larval skeletal elements entirely.
evidence: This is established knowledge about echinoderm larval anatomy.

claim: Holothuroids (sea cucumbers) have rudimentary skeletal elements.
source: The feeding larvae of echinoids (sea urchins) and ophiuroids (brittle stars) have extensive endoskeletons, holothuroids (sea cucumbers) have rudimentary skeletal elements, and asteroids (sea stars) lack larval skeletal elements entirely.
evidence: This is established knowledge about echinoderm larval anatomy.

claim: Asteroids (sea stars) lack larval skeletal elements entirely.
source: The feeding larvae of echinoids (sea urchins) and ophiuroids (brittle stars) have extensive endoskeletons, holothuroids (sea cucumbers) have rudimentary skeletal elements, and asteroids (sea stars) lack larval skeletal elements entirely.
evidence: This is established knowledge about echinoderm larval anatomy.

claim: Larval skeletons are thought to be derived within the echinoderms.
source: Larval skeletons are thought to be derived within the echinoderms as the feeding larvae of hemichordates (acorn worms), the sister group to echinoderms, and the larvae of crinoids (sea lilies and feather stars), a basal echinoderm clade, lack skeletons.
evidence: This is inferred from comparative anatomy and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: The feeding larvae of hemichordates (acorn worms), the sister group to echinoderms, lack skeletons.
source: Larval skeletons are thought to be derived within the echinoderms as the feeding larvae of hemichordates (acorn worms), the sister group to echinoderms, and the larvae of crinoids (sea lilies and feather stars), a basal echinoderm clade, lack skeletons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hemichordate anatomy.

claim: The larvae of crinoids (sea lilies and feather stars), a basal echinoderm clade, lack skeletons.
source: Larval skeletons are thought to be derived within the echinoderms as the feeding larvae of hemichordates (acorn worms), the sister group to echinoderms, and the larvae of crinoids (sea lilies and feather stars), a basal echinoderm clade, lack skeletons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about crinoid larval anatomy.

claim: The skeletal cells of larval and adult echinoderms are similar in many respects.
source: The skeletal cells of larval and adult echinoderms are similar in many respects, supporting the widely accepted view that the larval skeleton arose via co-option of the adult skeletogenic program (Czarkwiani et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2015; Gao and Davidson, 2008; Killian et al., 2010; Mann et al., 2010; Mann et al., 2008; Richardson et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior comparative studies.

claim: The larval skeleton arose via co-option of the adult skeletogenic program.
source: The skeletal cells of larval and adult echinoderms are similar in many respects, supporting the widely accepted view that the larval skeleton arose via co-option of the adult skeletogenic program (Czarkwiani et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2015; Gao and Davidson, 2008; Killian et al., 2010; Mann et al., 2010; Mann et al., 2008; Richardson et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and is a widely accepted view.

claim: The embryonic skeleton of euechinoid sea urchins is formed by a specialized population of skeletogenic cells known as primary mesenchyme cells (PMCs).
source: The embryonic skeleton of euechinoid sea urchins, the best studied taxon, is formed by a specialized population of skeletogenic cells known as primary mesenchyme cells (PMCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sea urchin development.

claim: PMCs are the progeny of the large micromeres (LMs), four cells that arise near the vegetal pole during early cleavage.
source: These cells are the progeny of the large micromeres (LMs), four cells that arise near the vegetal pole during early cleavage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sea urchin cell lineage.

claim: The GRN that underlies PMC specification is one of the best characterized GRNs in any animal embryo.
source: The GRN that underlies PMC specification is one of the best characterized GRNs in any animal embryo (Oliveri et al., 2008; Shashikant et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior comprehensive studies.

claim: The PMC GRN is initially deployed through the activity of a localized maternal protein, Dishevelled, which stabilizes β-catenin in the LM lineage.
source: This GRN is initially deployed through the activity of a localized maternal protein, Dishevelled, which stabilizes β-catenin in the LM lineage, leading to the early zygotic expression of a repressor, pmar1/micro1 (Logan et al., 1999; Nishimura et al., 2004; Oliveri et al., 2002; Peng and Wikramanayake, 2013; Weitzel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior molecular studies.

claim: Stabilization of β-catenin in the LM lineage leads to the early zygotic expression of a repressor, pmar1/micro1.
source: This GRN is initially deployed through the activity of a localized maternal protein, Dishevelled, which stabilizes β-catenin in the LM lineage, leading to the early zygotic expression of a repressor, pmar1/micro1 (Logan et al., 1999; Nishimura et al., 2004; Oliveri et al., 2002; Peng and Wikramanayake, 2013; Weitzel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior molecular studies.

claim: These molecular events lead to the zygotic expression of several regulatory genes selectively in the LM-PMC lineage.
source: These molecular events lead to the zygotic expression of several regulatory genes selectively in the LM-PMC lineage.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on the PMC GRN.

claim: alx1 and ets1 are two of the most important regulatory genes expressed in the LM-PMC lineage.
source: Two of the most important of these regulatory genes are alx1 (Ettensohn et al., 2003) and ets1 (Kurokawa et al., 1999), each of which is required for PMC specification and morphogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: alx1 is required for PMC specification and morphogenesis.
source: Two of the most important of these regulatory genes are alx1 (Ettensohn et al., 2003) and ets1 (Kurokawa et al., 1999), each of which is required for PMC specification and morphogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior functional studies.

claim: ets1 is required for PMC specification and morphogenesis.
source: Two of the most important of these regulatory genes are alx1 (Ettensohn et al., 2003) and ets1 (Kurokawa et al., 1999), each of which is required for PMC specification and morphogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior functional studies.

claim: After their specification, PMCs undergo a spectacular sequence of morphogenetic behaviors that includes epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), directional cell migration, cell fusion, and biomineral formation.
source: After their specification, PMCs undergo a spectacular sequence of morphogenetic behaviors that includes epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), directional cell migration, cell fusion, and biomineral formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PMC behavior.

claim: PMCs undergo EMT at the late blastula stage, ingressing from the vegetal plate into the blastocoel.
source: PMCs undergo EMT at the late blastula stage, ingressing from the vegetal plate into the blastocoel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PMC behavior.

claim: PMCs migrate along the blastocoel wall and gradually arrange themselves in a ring-like pattern near the equator of the embryo.
source: They migrate along the blastocoel wall and gradually arrange themselves in a ring-like pattern near the equator of the embryo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PMC behavior.

claim: As PMCs migrate, they extend filopodia that fuse with those of neighboring PMCs, giving rise to a cable-like structure that joins the cells in a single, extensive syncytium.
source: As they migrate, PMCs extend filopodia that fuse with those of neighboring PMCs, giving rise to a cable-like structure that joins the cells in a single, extensive syncytium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PMC behavior.

claim: Beginning late in gastrulation and continuing throughout the remainder of embryogenesis, PMCs deposit calcified biomineral within the syncytial filopodial cable.
source: Beginning late in gastrulation and continuing throughout the remainder of embryogenesis, PMCs deposit calcified biomineral within the syncytial filopodial cable.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PMC behavior.

claim: The complex sequence of PMC morphogenetic behaviors is regulated by hundreds of specialized effector proteins.
source: The complex sequence of PMC morphogenetic behaviors is regulated by hundreds of specialized effector proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the complexity of the morphogenetic process.

claim: The spatiotemporal expression patterns of PMC effector proteins are controlled by the GRN deployed in the LM-PMC lineage.
source: The spatiotemporal expression patterns of these proteins are controlled by the GRN deployed in the LM-PMC lineage.
evidence: This is a logical inference from GRN function.

claim: A major current goal is to identify effector proteins that regulate specific PMC behaviors and elucidate the GRN circuitry that controls these genes.
source: A major current goal is to identify effector proteins that regulate specific PMC behaviors and elucidate the GRN circuitry that controls these genes (see Ettensohn, 2013; Lyons et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior reviews.

claim: There is currently only a limited understanding of the cis-regulatory control of three PMC effector genes: sm30, sm50, and cyclophilin/cyp1.
source: At present, we have only a limited understanding of the cis-regulatory control of three PMC effector genes: two genes (sm30 and sm50) that encode secreted proteins occluded in the biomineral (Makabe et al., 1995; Walters et al., 2008) and a third gene (cyclophilin/cyp1) of unknown function (Amore and Davidson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: sm30 and sm50 encode secreted proteins occluded in the biomineral.
source: At present, we have only a limited understanding of the cis-regulatory control of three PMC effector genes: two genes (sm30 and sm50) that encode secreted proteins occluded in the biomineral (Makabe et al., 1995; Walters et al., 2008) and a third gene (cyclophilin/cyp1) of unknown function (Amore and Davidson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: cyclophilin/cyp1 is a PMC effector gene of unknown function.
source: At present, we have only a limited understanding of the cis-regulatory control of three PMC effector genes: two genes (sm30 and sm50) that encode secreted proteins occluded in the biomineral (Makabe et al., 1995; Walters et al., 2008) and a third gene (cyclophilin/cyp1) of unknown function (Amore and Davidson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: KirrelL is a PMC-specific, Ig domain-containing, transmembrane protein required for cell–cell fusion.
source: KirrelL is a PMC-specific, Ig domain-containing, transmembrane protein required for cell–cell fusion (Ettensohn and Dey, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior functional study.

claim: The expression and function of KirrelL have been examined in two sea urchin species, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and Lytechinus variegatus.
source: The expression and function of the protein have been examined in two sea urchin species, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and Lytechinus variegatus.
evidence: This is supported by prior research.

claim: In kirrelL morphants, PMCs extend filopodia and migrate but filopodial contacts do not result in fusion.
source: In kirrelL morphants, PMCs extend filopodia and migrate but filopodial contacts do not result in fusion; this prevents the formation of the PMC syncytium and results in the secretion of small, unconnected biomineralized elements.
evidence: This is supported by prior functional studies.

claim: Loss of kirrelL function prevents the formation of the PMC syncytium and results in the secretion of small, unconnected biomineralized elements.
source: In kirrelL morphants, PMCs extend filopodia and migrate but filopodial contacts do not result in fusion; this prevents the formation of the PMC syncytium and results in the secretion of small, unconnected biomineralized elements.
evidence: This is supported by prior functional studies.

claim: In all echinoderms that have been examined, the kirrelL gene lacks introns.
source: In all echinoderms that have been examined, the kirrelL gene lacks introns, raising the possibility that its origin early in echinoderm evolution was a consequence of retrotransposition, a common gene transfer mechanism that results in intronless genes and one that has played a particularly prominent role in the diversification of Ig-domain-containing proteins (Baertsch et al., 2008; Cordaux and Batzer, 2009; Dermody et al., 2009; Farré et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by genomic sequence analysis.

claim: The origin of kirrelL early in echinoderm evolution may have been a consequence of retrotransposition.
source: In all echinoderms that have been examined, the kirrelL gene lacks introns, raising the possibility that its origin early in echinoderm evolution was a consequence of retrotransposition, a common gene transfer mechanism that results in intronless genes and one that has played a particularly prominent role in the diversification of Ig-domain-containing proteins (Baertsch et al., 2008; Cordaux and Batzer, 2009; Dermody et al., 2009; Farré et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the intronless structure of the gene.

claim: Retrotransposition is a common gene transfer mechanism that results in intronless genes.
source: In all echinoderms that have been examined, the kirrelL gene lacks introns, raising the possibility that its origin early in echinoderm evolution was a consequence of retrotransposition, a common gene transfer mechanism that results in intronless genes and one that has played a particularly prominent role in the diversification of Ig-domain-containing proteins (Baertsch et al., 2008; Cordaux and Batzer, 2009; Dermody et al., 2009; Farré et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Retrotransposition has played a particularly prominent role in the diversification of Ig-domain-containing proteins.
source: In all echinoderms that have been examined, the kirrelL gene lacks introns, raising the possibility that its origin early in echinoderm evolution was a consequence of retrotransposition, a common gene transfer mechanism that results in intronless genes and one that has played a particularly prominent role in the diversification of Ig-domain-containing proteins (Baertsch et al., 2008; Cordaux and Batzer, 2009; Dermody et al., 2009; Farré et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In S. purpuratus, kirrelL expression is first detectable at the blastula stage (~18 hpf) and peaks early in gastrulation (~30 hpf).
source: In S. purpuratus, kirrelL expression is first detectable at the blastula stage (~18 hpf) and peaks early in gastrulation (~30 hpf) (Tu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior expression analysis.

claim: Sp-kirrelL expression declines after peaking at ~30 hpf and is followed by a second peak at ~64 hpf.
source: Expression then declines and is followed by a second peak at ~64 hpf, when kirrelL is expressed predominantly at sites of active skeletal rod growth as a consequence of localized, ectoderm-derived cues (Sun and Ettensohn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior expression analysis.

claim: At ~64 hpf, kirrelL is expressed predominantly at sites of active skeletal rod growth as a consequence of localized, ectoderm-derived cues.
source: Expression then declines and is followed by a second peak at ~64 hpf, when kirrelL is expressed predominantly at sites of active skeletal rod growth as a consequence of localized, ectoderm-derived cues (Sun and Ettensohn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: RNA-seq studies have shown that Sp-kirrelL is positively regulated both by Alx1 and Ets1.
source: RNA-seq studies have shown that Sp-kirrelL, like many PMC effector genes, is positively regulated both by Alx1 and Ets1 (Rafiq et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior RNA-seq study.

claim: kirrelL is expressed specifically in the embryonic skeletogenic mesenchyme of a brittle star, Amphiura filiformis.
source: Although the gene has only been studied in detail in sea urchins, a recent study found that kirrelL is also expressed specifically in the embryonic skeletogenic mesenchyme of a brittle star, Amphiura filiformis (Dylus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior expression study.

claim: Potential Sp-kirrelL CREs were identified based on whether candidate regions were hyperaccessible in PMCs relative to other cell types.
source: We identified potential Sp-kirrelL CREs based on several criteria. We considered whether candidate regions were (1) hyperaccessible in PMCs relative to other cell types, (2) bound by Alx1, a key transcription factor in the PMC GRN and a positive regulator of Sp-kirrelL, (3) associated with active enhancer RNA (eRNA) expression, and (4) phylogenetically conserved at the level of DNA sequence.
evidence: This describes the criteria used in the study.

claim: Potential Sp-kirrelL CREs were identified based on whether candidate regions were bound by Alx1.
source: We identified potential Sp-kirrelL CREs based on several criteria. We considered whether candidate regions were (1) hyperaccessible in PMCs relative to other cell types, (2) bound by Alx1, a key transcription factor in the PMC GRN and a positive regulator of Sp-kirrelL, (3) associated with active enhancer RNA (eRNA) expression, and (4) phylogenetically conserved at the level of DNA sequence.
evidence: This describes the criteria used in the study.

claim: Potential Sp-kirrelL CREs were identified based on whether candidate regions were associated with active enhancer RNA (eRNA) expression.
source: We identified potential Sp-kirrelL CREs based on several criteria. We considered whether candidate regions were (1) hyperaccessible in PMCs relative to other cell types, (2) bound by Alx1, a key transcription factor in the PMC GRN and a positive regulator of Sp-kirrelL, (3) associated with active enhancer RNA (eRNA) expression, and (4) phylogenetically conserved at the level of DNA sequence.
evidence: This describes the criteria used in the study.

claim: Potential Sp-kirrelL CREs were identified based on whether candidate regions were phylogenetically conserved at the level of DNA sequence.
source: We identified potential Sp-kirrelL CREs based on several criteria. We considered whether candidate regions were (1) hyperaccessible in PMCs relative to other cell types, (2) bound by Alx1, a key transcription factor in the PMC GRN and a positive regulator of Sp-kirrelL, (3) associated with active enhancer RNA (eRNA) expression, and (4) phylogenetically conserved at the level of DNA sequence.
evidence: This describes the criteria used in the study.

claim: ATAC-seq and DNase-seq were used to identify regions of chromatin that are differentially accessible in PMCs relative to other cell types at the mesenchyme blastula stage.
source: In a previous study, ATAC-seq and DNase-seq were used to identify regions of chromatin that are differentially accessible in PMCs relative to other cell types at the mesenchyme blastula stage (Shashikant et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: ChIP-seq was used to identify binding sites of Sp-Alx1 at the mesenchyme blastula stage.
source: ChIP-seq was used to identify binding sites of Sp-Alx1 at the same developmental stage (Khor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: CAGE-seq was used to profile eRNA expression at nine different stages of early sea urchin embryogenesis.
source: Recently, we used Cap Analysis of Gene Expression Sequencing (CAGE-seq) to profile eRNA expression at nine different stages of early sea urchin embryogenesis (Khor et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Integration of ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, ChIP-seq, and CAGE-seq datasets revealed several putative CREs located near Sp-kirrelL.
source: Significantly, our integration of these different genome-wide datasets revealed several putative CREs located near Sp-kirrelL, some of which were found to share several signatures (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the integration of multiple genomic datasets shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Developmental CAGE-seq profiles of eRNAs provided additional information regarding temporal patterns of CRE activity.
source: Developmental CAGE-seq profiles of eRNAs also provided additional information regarding temporal patterns of CRE activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the CAGE-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The intergenic sequences flanking Sp-kirrelL were divided into nine putative CREs (labeled elements A–I) based on cross-species sequence conservation, cell type-specific DNA accessibility, Sp-Alx1-binding, and eRNA expression.
source: Based on cross-species sequence conservation, cell type-specific DNA accessibility, Sp-Alx1-binding, and eRNA expression, we divided the intergenic sequences flanking Sp-kirrelL into nine putative CREs (labeled elements A–I) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The putative Sp-kirrelL CREs were between 1.0 and 2.4 kb in size, with an average size of 1.5 kb.
source: The elements were between 1.0 and 2.4 kb in size, with an average size of 1.5 kb.
evidence: This is based on the size of the identified elements.

claim: A GFP reporter construct containing upstream elements A–G recapitulated the correct spatial expression pattern of endogenous Sp-kirrelL with minimal ectopic expression.
source: We observed that a GFP reporter construct containing upstream elements A–G recapitulated the correct spatial expression pattern of endogenous Sp-kirrelL with minimal ectopic expression (Figure 2B, C and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A reporter construct containing elements D–G drove strong GFP expression specifically in PMCs.
source: Further dissections revealed that a reporter construct containing elements D–G also drove strong GFP expression specifically in PMCs while a construct consisting of elements A–C showed weak GFP expression in PMCs.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: A construct consisting of elements A–C showed weak GFP expression in PMCs.
source: Further dissections revealed that a reporter construct containing elements D–G also drove strong GFP expression specifically in PMCs while a construct consisting of elements A–C showed weak GFP expression in PMCs.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: When elements were tested individually, only elements C and G were able to drive GFP expression in sea urchin embryos.
source: When elements were tested individually, we found that only elements C and G were able to drive GFP expression in sea urchin embryos.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: Element G drove strong GFP expression specifically in the PMCs.
source: Element G, which is directly upstream of the Sp-kirrelL translational start site and contains part of the Sp-kirrelL 5′ untranslated region (UTR), was observed to drive strong GFP expression specifically in the PMCs.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: Element G is directly upstream of the Sp-kirrelL translational start site and contains part of the Sp-kirrelL 5′ UTR.
source: Element G, which is directly upstream of the Sp-kirrelL translational start site and contains part of the Sp-kirrelL 5′ untranslated region (UTR), was observed to drive strong GFP expression specifically in the PMCs.
evidence: This is based on genomic location analysis.

claim: Element C drove GFP expression specifically in the PMCs, although fewer embryos expressed detectable levels of the reporter compared to element G.
source: Element C was also observed to drive GFP expression specifically in the PMCs, although fewer embryos expressed detectable levels of the reporter.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: Element C is differentially accessible in the PMCs based on both ATAC-seq and DNase-seq.
source: Element C is noteworthy as it is differentially accessible in the PMCs based on both ATAC-seq and DNase-seq, bound by Sp-Alx1, and associated with eRNA expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Element C is bound by Sp-Alx1.
source: Element C is noteworthy as it is differentially accessible in the PMCs based on both ATAC-seq and DNase-seq, bound by Sp-Alx1, and associated with eRNA expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Element C is associated with eRNA expression.
source: Element C is noteworthy as it is differentially accessible in the PMCs based on both ATAC-seq and DNase-seq, bound by Sp-Alx1, and associated with eRNA expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by CAGE-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A reporter construct containing element C alone showed relatively weak reporter activity, similar to the construct containing elements A–C.
source: We found that a reporter construct containing element C alone showed relatively weak reporter activity, similar to the construct containing elements A–C.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: A larger, overlapping CRE termed BC.ATAC, which included part, but not all, of element C, exhibited strikingly enhanced GFP expression in PMCs.
source: In contrast, a larger, overlapping CRE we termed BC.ATAC, which included part, but not all, of element C, exhibited strikingly enhanced GFP expression in PMCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The difference in activity between element C and BC.ATAC suggested that element C might contain regulatory sites that have greater activity when in close proximity to the promoter.
source: This difference in activity between element C and BC.ATAC suggested that element C might contain regulatory sites that have greater activity when in close proximity to the promoter.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in reporter activity.

claim: The minimal element C region that showed strong, PMC-specific activity was determined to be C.ChIP.
source: The minimal element C region that showed strong, PMC-specific activity was determined to be C.ChIP.
evidence: This is supported by truncation analysis of element C.

claim: Increasing the distance between the C.ChIP element and the promoter (as in the C.DNase construct) significantly reduced enhancer activity.
source: Increasing the distance between the C.ChIP element and the promoter (as in the C.DNase construct) significantly reduced enhancer activity.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: JASPAR was used to predict transcription factor inputs within C.ChIP, with a focus on transcription factors known to be expressed at higher levels in PMCs than in other cell types.
source: To predict transcription factor inputs within C.ChIP, we scanned the 200 bp C.ChIP sequence using JASPAR (Mathelier et al., 2016), with a focus on transcription factors known to be expressed at higher levels in PMCs than in other cell types.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis performed.

claim: JASPAR analysis identified several candidate Alx1- and Ets1-binding sites in element C.ChIP.
source: This analysis identified several candidate Alx1- and Ets1-binding sites (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WMISH analysis of alx1 and ets1 morphants confirmed that Sp-kirrelL expression declined to undetectable levels.
source: Consistent with previous RNA-seq analysis which has shown that Sp-kirrelL is sensitive to alx1 and ets1 knockdowns (Rafiq et al., 2014), our whole-mount in situ hybridization (WMISH) analysis of both alx1 and ets1 morphants confirmed that Sp-kirrelL expression declined to undetectable levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by WMISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutations of all putative Alx1- and/or Ets1-binding sites in C.ChIP completely abolished GFP expression.
source: Our mutational analysis of C.ChIP revealed that mutations of all putative Alx1- and/or Ets1-binding sites completely abolished GFP expression (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Constructs containing mutations in putative Fox- or MEIS-binding sites in C.ChIP exhibited reporter activity similar to that of the parental construct.
source: In contrast, constructs containing mutations in putative Fox- or MEIS-binding sites exhibited reporter activity similar to that of the parental construct.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis.

claim: Mutations of individual Alx1 and Ets1 sites in C.ChIP revealed that Alx1 half site 2 and Ets1 site 1 provided key regulatory inputs.
source: Mutations of individual Alx1 and Ets1 sites revealed that Alx1 half site 2 and Ets1 site 1 provided key regulatory inputs.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis.

claim: A 301-bp region surrounding the transcriptional start site, considered to include the Sp-kirrelL core promoter, drove ectopic GFP expression when tested in the EpGFPII plasmid.
source: When tested in the EpGFPII plasmid, we found that a 301-bp region surrounding the transcriptional start site, a region we considered to include the Sp-kirrelL core promoter, drove ectopic GFP expression.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: The same 301-bp element failed to drive significant reporter expression in a BAC construct, indicating that the activity of the 310-bp element in EpGFPII was the result of abnormal synergy between the Sp-kirrelL and Sp-endo16 promoters.
source: As shown below, however, the same element failed to drive significant reporter expression in a BAC construct, indicating that the activity of the 310-bp element in EpGFPII was the result of abnormal synergy between the Sp-kirrelL and Sp-endo16 promoters.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in activity between plasmid and BAC constructs.

claim: The minimal element G fragment that drove strongest PMC-specific GFP expression is G.ATAC.
source: We next performed mutational analysis of the minimal element G fragment that drove strongest PMC-specific GFP expression (G.ATAC).
evidence: This is supported by truncation analysis.

claim: G.ATAC receives direct and positive inputs from Alx1 and Ets1.
source: We determined that this CRE receives direct and positive inputs from Alx1 and Ets1, similar to the C.ChIP element (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: For two constructs in which all Alx1- or all Ets1-binding sites in G.ATAC were mutated, the difference in the numbers of embryos that exhibited PMC-specific versus ectopic expression as compared to the parental G.ATAC construct was highly significant by a chi-square test (p < 0.001).
source: For two constructs in which all Alx1- or all Ets1-binding sites were mutated, the difference in the numbers of embryos that exhibited PMC-specific versus ectopic expression as compared to the parental G.ATAC construct (see Figure 2—source data 1) was highly significant by a chi-square test (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: Reporter constructs with mutated CEBPA-, Fos::Jun-, Fox-, MEIS-, or Tbrain-binding sites in G.ATAC exhibited PMC-specific GFP expression similar to that of the parental construct.
source: Reporter constructs with mutated CEBPA-, Fos::Jun-, Fox-, MEIS-, or Tbrain-binding sites exhibited PMC-specific GFP expression similar to that of the parental construct.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis.

claim: Different Sp-kirrelL element G truncations injected into fertilized L. variegatus eggs exhibited similar expression patterns to those observed in S. purpuratus, indicating that inputs into element G are conserved in these two sea urchin species.
source: We also injected the different Sp-kirrelL element G truncations into fertilized L. variegatus eggs and observed similar expression patterns, indicating that inputs into element G are conserved in these two sea urchin species (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by cross-species transgenic reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Several CREs (elements B, C, E, F, H, and I) were individually able to drive strong PMC-specific GFP expression when cloned adjacent to the native Sp-kirrelL promoter.
source: Strikingly, we found that elements B, C, E, F, H, and I were individually able to drive strong PMC-specific GFP expression when cloned adjacent to the Sp-kirrelL promoter, although these elements had previously exhibited minimal activity in the context of the Sp-endo16 promoter alone (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4D; compared to Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data shown in Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Elements B, C, E, F, H, and I had previously exhibited minimal activity in the context of the Sp-endo16 promoter alone.
source: Strikingly, we found that elements B, C, E, F, H, and I were individually able to drive strong PMC-specific GFP expression when cloned adjacent to the Sp-kirrelL promoter, although these elements had previously exhibited minimal activity in the context of the Sp-endo16 promoter alone (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4D; compared to Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: Element C in combination with the Sp-endo16 promoter drove GFP expression in only 8.6% of embryos.
source: As an example, element C in combination with the Sp-endo16 promoter drove GFP expression in only 8.6% of embryos, the Sp-kirrelL promoter region in combination with the Sp-endo16 promoter drove GFP expression in 19% of the embryos, but the combination of element C with the two promoter elements drove expression in 37.8% of embryos (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: The Sp-kirrelL promoter region in combination with the Sp-endo16 promoter drove GFP expression in 19% of the embryos.
source: As an example, element C in combination with the Sp-endo16 promoter drove GFP expression in only 8.6% of embryos, the Sp-kirrelL promoter region in combination with the Sp-endo16 promoter drove GFP expression in 19% of the embryos, but the combination of element C with the two promoter elements drove expression in 37.8% of embryos (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: The combination of element C with the Sp-kirrelL and Sp-endo16 promoter elements drove expression in 37.8% of embryos.
source: As an example, element C in combination with the Sp-endo16 promoter drove GFP expression in only 8.6% of embryos, the Sp-kirrelL promoter region in combination with the Sp-endo16 promoter drove GFP expression in 19% of the embryos, but the combination of element C with the two promoter elements drove expression in 37.8% of embryos (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: The elevated expression of the construct containing element C with both promoter elements indicated that its activity was not due solely to the additive activity of the C and Sp-kirrelL promoter elements interacting independently with the Sp-endo16 promoter.
source: The elevated expression of the latter construct indicated that the its activity was not due solely to the additive activity of the C and SpkirrelL promoter elements interacting independently with the Sp-endo16 promoter (37.8 > 8.6 + 19).
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative comparison of reporter activities.

claim: The C element exhibited substantial activity in the context of the Sp-kirrelL promoter alone, in the absence of the Sp-endo16 promoter.
source: In addition, we found that the C element exhibited substantial activity in the context of the Sp-kirrelL promoter alone, in the absence of the Sp-endo16 promoter (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The presence of the native Sp-kirrelL promoter mitigated the need for the C.ChIP element within element C to be adjacent to the promoter for strong PMC-specific GFP expression.
source: We also observed that the presence of the native Sp-kirrelL promoter mitigated the need for the C.ChIP element within element C to be adjacent to the promoter for strong PMC-specific GFP expression.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: Enhancer activity was dependent on the sequence of the Sp-kirrelL promoter, as GFP expression was abolished in a construct where the sequence was shuffled.
source: We confirmed that enhancer activity was dependent on the sequence of the Sp-kirrelL promoter, as GFP expression was abolished in a construct where the sequence was shuffled (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Insertion of a scrambled sequence between C.ChIP and the promoter decreased activity compared to when C.ChIP was directly adjacent to the promoter.
source: We found that insertion of this sequence decreased activity compared to when C.ChIP was directly adjacent to the promoter.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: The principle effect of deleting the region between C.ChIP and the promoter was to decrease the spacing between C.Chip and the promoter rather than removing repressor sites.
source: This supports the view that the principle effect of deleting this region was to decrease the spacing between C.Chip and the promoter rather than removing repressor sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of inserting a scrambled sequence.

claim: Several CREs are capable of functioning in concert specifically with the native Sp-kirrelL promoter and this can bypass spacing hurdles that are evident when the Sp-endo16 promoter alone is present.
source: Taken together, these findings showed that several CREs are capable of functioning in concert specifically with the native Sp-kirrelL promoter and that this can bypass spacing hurdles that are evident when the Sp-endo16 promoter alone is present.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of transgenic reporter assays.

claim: A 130-kb BAC containing the single exon Sp-kirrelL gene, flanked by 65 kb of sequences in each direction, was used to explore the relative contributions of various elements to Sp-kirrelL expression in vivo.
source: For these studies, we utilized a 130-kb BAC that contained the single exon Sp-kirrelL gene, flanked by 65 kb of sequences in each direction.
evidence: This describes the BAC construct used in the study.

claim: Recombination-mediated genetic engineering (recombineering) was used to replace the single Sp-kirrelL exon seamlessly with either GFP or mCherry coding sequence.
source: We used recombination-mediated genetic engineering (recombineering) to replace the single Sp-kirrelL exon seamlessly with either GFP or mCherry coding sequence (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate BAC reporters.

claim: Sp.kirrelL.mCherry.BAC faithfully recapitulated the expression of endogenous Sp-kirrelL in the PMCs at 48 hpf with minimal ectopic expression.
source: We found that Sp.kirrelL.mCherry.BAC faithfully recapitulated the expression of endogenous Sp-kirrelL in the PMCs at 48 hpf with minimal ectopic expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by BAC reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of elements A–G (ΔCRE.GFP.BAC) completely abolished GFP expression.
source: We found that deletion of elements A–G (ΔCRE.GFP.BAC) completely abolished GFP expression.
evidence: This is supported by BAC deletion analysis.

claim: Retaining the minimal endogenous Sp-kirrelL promoter (ΔCRE.kirrelLprm.GFP.BAC) did not rescue GFP expression.
source: We also observed that retaining the minimal endogenous Sp-kirrelL promoter (ΔCRE.kirrelLprm.GFP.BAC) did not rescue GFP expression, demonstrating that elements A–G are necessary for PMC-specific Sp-kirrelL expression in the context of the Sp.kirrelL.GFP.BAC consistent with our previous, plasmid-based analysis.
evidence: This is supported by BAC deletion analysis.

claim: Elements A–G are necessary for PMC-specific Sp-kirrelL expression in the context of the Sp.kirrelL.GFP.BAC.
source: We also observed that retaining the minimal endogenous Sp-kirrelL promoter (ΔCRE.kirrelLprm.GFP.BAC) did not rescue GFP expression, demonstrating that elements A–G are necessary for PMC-specific Sp-kirrelL expression in the context of the Sp.kirrelL.GFP.BAC consistent with our previous, plasmid-based analysis.
evidence: This is supported by BAC deletion analysis.

claim: A BAC containing deletion of element G (ΔG.GFP.BAC, which included a deletion of the Sp-kirrelL promoter) abolished GFP expression at 48 hpf.
source: We found that a BAC containing deletion of the element G (ΔG.GFP.BAC, which included a deletion of the Sp-kirrelL promoter) abolished GFP expression at 48 hpf (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by BAC deletion analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of all of element G except for the promoter region (ΔG.kirrelLpromoter.GFP.BAC) resulted in a GFP spatial expression pattern similar to that of the parental mCherry.
source: By contrast, deletion of all of element G except for the promoter region (ΔG.kirrelLpromoter.GFP.BAC), resulted in a GFP spatial expression pattern similar to that of the parental mCherry.
evidence: This is supported by BAC deletion analysis.

claim: The Sp-kirrelL promoter is essential for PMC-specific expression even when all distal CREs are present.
source: These findings confirmed the importance of the Sp-kirrelL promoter in supporting PMC-specific expression of the gene and showed that this region is essential even when all distal CREs are present.
evidence: This is inferred from the BAC deletion analysis.

claim: BACs containing individual deletions of elements other than G all remained active at 48 hpf and supported PMC-specific reporter expression.
source: BACs containing individual deletions of other elements all remained active at 48 hpf and supported PMC-specific reporter expression, pointing to considerable redundancy in the contribution of each element to Sp-kirrelL expression.
evidence: This is supported by BAC deletion analysis.

claim: There is considerable redundancy in the contribution of each element to Sp-kirrelL expression.
source: BACs containing individual deletions of other elements all remained active at 48 hpf and supported PMC-specific reporter expression, pointing to considerable redundancy in the contribution of each element to Sp-kirrelL expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the BAC deletion analysis.

claim: Deletion of element C resulted in approximately a 50% reduction in expression compared to WT BAC.
source: We found that deletion of element C resulted in approximately a 50% reduction in expression compared to WT BAC.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative NanoString analysis.

claim: GFP expression was completely abolished when element G was deleted (ΔG.GFP.BAC).
source: As we observed previously, GFP expression was completely abolished when element G was deleted (ΔG.GFP.BAC) and this effect was diminished when the Sp-kirrelL promoter was retained (ΔG.kirrelLprm.GFP.BAC).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative NanoString analysis.

claim: Retention of the Sp-kirrelL promoter alone resulted in only a partial rescue of expression, with overall levels reduced substantially compared to the wild-type BAC.
source: Quantitative analysis revealed, however, that retention of the Sp-kirrelL promoter alone resulted in only a partial rescue of expression, with overall levels reduced substantially compared to the wild-type BAC.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative NanoString analysis.

claim: Deletion of element H resulted in decreased expression levels.
source: We also observed that deletion of element H resulted in decreased expression levels.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative NanoString analysis.

claim: At early stages of embryo development, Sp-kirrelL expression is controlled by multiple CREs, notably the C, G, and H modules, acting in concert with the Sp-kirrelL promoter.
source: Taken together, our qualitative and quantitative analyses show that at early stages of embryo development, Sp-kirrelL expression is controlled by multiple CREs, notably the C, G, and H modules, acting in concert with the Sp-kirrelL promoter.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of BAC deletion and quantitative analysis.

claim: Noncoding sequences (~1- to 2-kb) directly upstream of the translational start sites of kirrelL genes from Eucidaris tribuloides, Parastichopus parvimensis, P. miniata, Acanthaster planci, Ophionereis fasciata, and Anneissia japonica were cloned into the EpGFPII plasmid and injected into fertilized S. purpuratus eggs.
source: We cloned ~1- to 2-kb noncoding sequences (see Figure 6—source data 1 and Figure 6—source data 2) directly upstream of the translational start sites of kirrelL genes from Eucidaris tribuloides (pencil urchin), Parastichopus parvimensis (sea cucumber), P. miniata (sea star), Acanthaster planci (crown-of-thorns starfish), Ophionereis fasciata (brittle star), and Anneissia japonica (feather star) into the EpGFPII plasmid and injected them into fertilized S. purpuratus eggs (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the cross-species analysis performed.

claim: All six heterologous kirrelL regulatory regions drove GFP expression in sea urchin embryos, with five out of six exhibiting strong GFP expression selectively in PMCs.
source: Remarkably, we found that all six drove GFP expression in sea urchin embryos, with five out of six exhibiting strong GFP expression selectively in PMCs (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by cross-species transgenic reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: kirrelL CREs across echinoderm species are highly conserved in function.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that kirrelL CREs across echinoderm species are highly conserved in function.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-species transgenic reporter assay results.

claim: kirrelL CREs from deeply divergent echinoderm species that do not form embryonic or larval skeletons (sea stars and feather stars) drive PMC-selective GFP expression in sea urchin embryos.
source: We found it particularly striking that kirrelL CREs from deeply divergent echinoderm species that do not form embryonic or larval skeletons (sea stars and feather stars) drive PMC-selective GFP expression in sea urchin embryos.
evidence: This is supported by cross-species transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: Lv-kirrelL is expressed in the skeletogenic centers of the adult rudiment and in the spine of 5-week-old juvenile sea urchins.
source: We observed Lv-kirrelL expression in the skeletogenic centers of the adult rudiment and in the spine of 5-week-old juvenile sea urchins (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by WMISH data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The expression pattern of Lv-kirrelL was very similar to that of Lv-msp130r2, a highly expressed biomineralization gene.
source: The expression pattern of Lv-kirrelL was very similar to that of Lv-msp130r2, a highly expressed biomineralization gene (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of WMISH data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Pm-kirrelL expression was not detected during early embryonic and larval development in P. miniata.
source: In contrast, expression of Pm-kirrelL was not detected during early embryonic and larval development in P. miniata, which does not from a larval skeleton (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by WMISH data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pm-kirrelL is expressed in the developing adult rudiment in premetamorphic, late-stage sea star larva and in the adult skeletogenic centers in juvenile sea stars.
source: Pm-kirrelL is, however, expressed in the developing adult rudiment in premetamorphic, late-stage sea star larva and in the adult skeletogenic centers in juvenile sea stars (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by WMISH data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pm-ets1 is expressed in the mesenchyme cells during early development and in the adult rudiment and skeletogenic centers in juvenile sea stars.
source: As a control, we showed Pm-ets1 expression in the mesenchyme cells during early development and an expression pattern in the adult rudiment and skeletogenic centers in juvenile sea stars that closely resembled that of Pm-kirrelL (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by WMISH data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Activity of the Pm-kirrelL CRE was restricted to the proximal region (Pm2).
source: Subdivision of the ~4 kb Pm-kirrelL regulatory region showed that activity was restricted to the proximal region (Pm2), and further analysis revealed that a 614-bp region (PmG) was sufficient to drive strong PMC-specific GFP expression in S. purpuratus embryos (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by truncation analysis shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A 614-bp region (PmG) was sufficient to drive strong PMC-specific GFP expression in S. purpuratus embryos.
source: Subdivision of the ~4 kb Pm-kirrelL regulatory region showed that activity was restricted to the proximal region (Pm2), and further analysis revealed that a 614-bp region (PmG) was sufficient to drive strong PMC-specific GFP expression in S. purpuratus embryos (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by truncation analysis shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Phylogenetic footprinting of genomic sequences from P. miniata and the closely related crown-of-thorns starfish (A. planci) showed substantial similarity in the PmG region.
source: Phylogenetic footprinting of genomic sequences from P. miniata and the closely related crown-of-thorns starfish (A. planci) showed substantial similarity in this region (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic footprinting analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The PmG element receives positive inputs from both Alx1 and Ets1.
source: We performed mutational analysis of the PmG element and found that this CRE receives positive inputs from both Alx1 and Ets1 (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A, B), similar to the Sp-kirrelL C and G.ATAC elements.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: For two constructs in which all Alx1- or all Ets1-binding sites in PmG were mutated, the difference in the numbers of embryos that exhibited PMC-specific versus ectopic expression as compared to the parental PmG construct was highly significant by a chi-square test (p < 0.001).
source: For two constructs in which all Alx1- or all Ets1-binding sites were mutated, the difference in the numbers of embryos that exhibited PMC-specific versus ectopic expression as compared to the parental PmG construct (see Figure 2—source data 1) was highly significant by a chi-square test (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: PmG1 and PmG2 elements were both interchangeable with the Sp-kirrelL promoter.
source: We found that PmG1 and PmG2 were both interchangeable with the Sp-kirrelL promoter and that interactions between SpC and PmG1 or PmG2 supported strong PMC-specific GFP expression in S. purpuratus embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric reporter construct analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Interactions between SpC and PmG1 or PmG2 supported strong PMC-specific GFP expression in S. purpuratus embryos.
source: We found that PmG1 and PmG2 were both interchangeable with the Sp-kirrelL promoter and that interactions between SpC and PmG1 or PmG2 supported strong PMC-specific GFP expression in S. purpuratus embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric reporter construct analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: PmG1 and PmG2 each conferred a roughly similar increase in expression frequency and specificity to element C as the Sp-kirrelL promoter region.
source: PmG1 and PmG2 each conferred a roughly similar increase in expression frequency and specificity to element C as the Sp-kirrelL promoter region (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: In a construct containing a PmG2 element with shuffled sequence, GFP expression was abolished.
source: In a construct containing a PmG2 element with shuffled sequence, GFP expression was abolished.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assay data.

claim: Knockdown of Alx1 or Ets1 expression substantially suppresses the activity of all constructs in PMCs.
source: We confirmed that knockdown of Alx1 or Ets1 expression substantially suppresses the activity of all constructs in PMCs.
evidence: This is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: There is a striking conservation of sequence and function in kirrelL promoters from deeply divergent echinoderm species.
source: These observations highlight a striking conservation of sequence and function in kirrelL promoters from deeply divergent echinoderm species.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-species analysis of kirrelL regulatory regions.

claim: The identification of Alx1 and Ets1 inputs into the Pm-kirrelL regulatory region provides evidence that these inputs are required in skeletal cells of the adult sea star.
source: Thus, our identification of Alx1 and Ets1 inputs into the Pm-kirrelL regulatory region provides evidence that these inputs are required in skeletal cells of the adult sea star, consistent with the finding that both Ets1 and Alx1 are expressed selectively by these cells (Gao and Davidson, 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the functional analysis of the Pm-kirrelL regulatory region and supported by citation to prior expression studies.

claim: Both Ets1 and Alx1 are expressed selectively by adult skeletal cells in sea stars.
source: Thus, our identification of Alx1 and Ets1 inputs into the Pm-kirrelL regulatory region provides evidence that these inputs are required in skeletal cells of the adult sea star, consistent with the finding that both Ets1 and Alx1 are expressed selectively by these cells (Gao and Davidson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior expression study.

claim: The findings provide the first glimpse of functional gene interactions in the ancestral, adult echinoderm skeletogenic program.
source: We propose instead that our findings provide the first glimpse of functional gene interactions in the ancestral, adult echinoderm skeletogenic program and highlight the remarkable conservation of this program in adults and embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the Pm-kirrelL regulatory region.

claim: The ancestral adult echinoderm skeletogenic program is remarkably conserved in adults and embryos.
source: We propose instead that our findings provide the first glimpse of functional gene interactions in the ancestral, adult echinoderm skeletogenic program and highlight the remarkable conservation of this program in adults and embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of kirrelL regulatory regions across echinoderms.

claim: Ets1 is expressed in the embryonic mesenchyme of modern sea stars.
source: As Ets1 is expressed in the embryonic mesenchyme of modern sea stars (Koga et al., 2010; McCauley et al., 2010), our findings support the view that a major event in the co-option of the adult skeletogenic GRN into the embryo was a heterochronic shift in the expression of Alx1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior expression studies.

claim: A major event in the co-option of the adult skeletogenic GRN into the embryo was a heterochronic shift in the expression of Alx1.
source: As Ets1 is expressed in the embryonic mesenchyme of modern sea stars (Koga et al., 2010; McCauley et al., 2010), our findings support the view that a major event in the co-option of the adult skeletogenic GRN into the embryo was a heterochronic shift in the expression of Alx1.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of Alx1 and Ets1 inputs into kirrelL and the expression patterns of these transcription factors.

claim: A heterochronic shift in Alx1 expression would have been sufficient to transfer a large part of the skeletogenic GRN into the embryo, as the transcription of many key effector genes, including kirrelL, was already directly linked to Alx1 and Ets1 expression.
source: This would have been sufficient to transfer a large part of the skeletogenic GRN into the embryo, as the transcription of many key effector genes, including kirrelL, was already directly linked to Alx1 and Ets1 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the regulatory architecture of kirrelL and other effector genes.
